terms.definition: A broad field evolved since the 1950s focused on making machines perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as recognizing images, understanding language, and making decisions.
terms.example: Computer vision, smart devices, and ML are all examples of AI

terms.definition: A subset of AI that uses existing data to train a mathematical model. The model learns patterns in training data so it can make accurate predictions on new input.
terms.example: Training a model on thousands of cat and dog photos so it can identify new ones

terms.definition: The process of feeding labeled data to an ML model repeatedly so it adjusts its internal parameters (weights) to minimize prediction errors.
terms.example: Showing a model 10,000 images of pizza until it learns what pizza looks like

terms.definition: The output an ML model produces by applying what it learned during training to new, previously unseen input data. Also called a prediction.
terms.example: A trained pizza classifier examining a new photo and predicting 'pizza' or 'not pizza'

terms.definition: A large AI model pre-trained on broad, diverse datasets that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks using prompts or fine-tuning.
terms.example: GPT-4, Claude, and Amazon Nova are all foundation models

terms.definition: A foundation model pre-trained on massive amounts of text (trillions of words) that can generate, summarize, translate, and converse in human language.
terms.example: Claude, GPT-4, Llama are LLMs; they power chatbots and code generators

terms.definition: A category of AI that can generate new content — text, images, audio, code — based on patterns learned from training data, in response to a prompt.
terms.example: Asking an AI to write a blog post or generate an image of a cat

terms.definition: An instruction or question written in natural language that a user provides to a generative AI model to request a specific output or task.
terms.example: 'Summarize the differences between dogs and cats' is a language prompt

terms.definition: When an AI model generates confident-sounding but factually incorrect or completely fabricated information. A known failure mode of LLMs.
terms.example: An AI citing a legal case that does not actually exist

terms.definition: A training problem where a model learns the training data too precisely — including its noise — and fails to generalize correctly to new, unseen examples.
terms.example: A student who memorizes exam answers but fails when questions are reworded

terms.definition: The numerical values (weights) inside an ML model that are adjusted during training to capture patterns. Modern LLMs have billions or trillions of parameters.
terms.example: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters; each one contributes to predictions

terms.definition: Systematic errors in AI outputs caused by imbalanced, non-representative, or prejudiced training data that leads to unfair or inaccurate results for certain groups.
terms.example: A facial recognition system trained mostly on one demographic misidentifying people from another

terms.definition: A framework requiring AI systems to be accurate, fair, safe, secure, explainable, transparent, governed, and controlled to minimize harm and ensure trust.
terms.example: Adding audit trails and human review processes to an AI hiring tool

terms.definition: An AWS managed service that provides access to multiple foundation models from AWS and third parties via a single API, abstracting infrastructure while enabling model customization.
terms.example: Using Bedrock to call Anthropic Claude or AWS Nova models without managing servers

terms.definition: AWS's comprehensive ML platform (analogous to IaaS) that provides full control over compute, data preparation, model training, and deployment pipelines.
terms.example: Using SageMaker Canvas to train a pizza/not-pizza image classifier

terms.definition: An AWS agentic AI tool that acts as an intelligent assistant for workplace tasks — summarizing documents, scheduling meetings, posting to Slack, and analyzing data.
terms.example: Asking Amazon Q to compare exam results across five CSV files in 30 seconds

terms.definition: A free AWS playground built on Bedrock that lets anyone experiment with AI models and build simple AI applications without coding or infrastructure setup.
terms.example: Building a chatbot demo or trying different models on PartyRock before touching Bedrock APIs

terms.definition: AI systems that can take autonomous actions, use tools, access external data, and make sequential decisions to accomplish a goal — going beyond simple question-and-answer.
terms.example: An AI agent that reads your calendar, finds a free slot, and sends meeting invites automatically

terms.definition: An AWS AI coding agent that helps developers write, review, and refactor code through natural language instructions, analogous to a higher-level programming abstraction.
terms.example: Telling Kiro to 'build a data validation pipeline' and receiving working Python code

terms.definition: The AWS SDK (Software Development Kit) for Python. Named after the Amazon river dolphin, it lets Python developers call AWS APIs to interact with services like SageMaker, Bedrock, and S3.
terms.example: Using boto3 in a Python script to invoke a SageMaker endpoint and classify an image

terms.definition: Multi-dimensional numerical representations (often 32-bit floating point numbers) that capture the semantic meaning and relationships between words or concepts in an ML model.
terms.example: The word 'king' and 'queen' will have similar vector embeddings because they are semantically related

terms.definition: The process of taking a pre-trained model and training it further on a smaller, domain-specific dataset to improve its performance on a particular task.
terms.example: Taking a general LLM and fine-tuning it on medical records to make it a better medical assistant

terms.definition: The basic unit of text that LLMs process — roughly equivalent to a word or a word fragment. Models are billed and context-limited based on token counts.
terms.example: The sentence 'Hello, world!' might be tokenized into 3-4 tokens
